newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus missing deal hailed as breakthrough, official.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus missing deal hailed as breakthrough, official.

text.p: A Cypriot official on Friday hailed as "the most significant breakthrough" an agreement that could lead to the opening of unmarked graves of persons missing in hostilities between Cyprus's Greek and Turkish communities.
But relatives expressed suspicion on the implications of the accord, announced after a meeting late on Thursday between Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
"We don't just want black bags full of remains. We need to find out what happened to them," said Nick Theodossiou, chairman of the committee of relatives of missing Greek Cypriots.
"What we want to avoid is going through mass graves ignoring some basic procedures. The rights of the missing persons and the rights of relatives must be respected."

But analysts and officials say the agreement is a major breakthrough in the issue which has plagued the divided Mediterranean island for decades, and one which is still considered a major hurdle in efforts to resolve the protracted Cyprus dispute.

"I was stunned. This is the most significant breakthrough in the issue of missing persons since 1974. I hope it leads to a breakthrough on other issues as well," a senior Greek Cypriot official told Reuters.
Under terms of the deal, the two sides will exchange information on the whereabouts of graves presumed to belong to missing persons, and expedite the return of remains to relatives.
The deal basically adopts a position that Clerides has been advocating for years on the simultaneous opening of graves on either side of the barbed wire on the "Green Line" that divides Cyprus.

The Greek Cypriot side says 1,619 Greek Cypriots are missing since 1974, when Turkish troops invaded and occupied the northern third of Cyprus after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
Many of them were said to have been alive after the cessation of hostilities.
Turkish Cypriots say 803 of their community are missing from intercommunal clashes dating back to the 1960s.

"I don't want to have the same fate as my father. We don't trust the Greeks and Greek Cypriots. We don't want bones. Can they give us our father back?" said Huseyin Herguner, a 35-year-old technician.
His father, Ahmet Cemal Herguner, went missing in 1974, taken away by Greeks between the first and second operations by Turkish mainland troops.

Takis Christopoulos, Presidential Commissioner for Humanitarian Affairs, told Reuters that a DNA bank currently in the making has gathered some 600 specimens from relatives of missing, and by September the work will be almost complete.
A tripartite committee working under U.N. auspices from the early 1980s has failed to provide conclusive evidence on the fate of any missing person.
Both leaders asked the U.N. Secretary-General to appoint a new third member to expedite the work of the committee. The position has been vacant for months.
